newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS-Nomura set to take majority in Czech IPB.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Nomura set to take majority in Czech IPB.

text.p: The Czech government has paved the way for Nomura International Plc to take a majority share in the country's third largest bank, IPB a.s., Finance Minister Ivan Pilip said on Thursday.
Pilip said Nomura had agreed to pay about six billion crowns ($175 million) for the state's 36 percent stake in IPB and would raise the bank's basic capital by a further six billion crowns.

"This share will be sold for the bourse price from the day of the offer which was 285 crowns... That is ... almost six billion crowns," Pilip told a news conference. "Nomura will raise the basic capital of the bank with a new issue of a further six billion crowns."

With the five percent share in IPB which Nomura already controls, through the Czech-registered firm Nutshell s.r.o., Pilip said Nomura "should have a majority share" when the equity sale and the basic capital increase have been completed.

Late on Wednesday, the government chose a bid by Nomura over one by Dutch ING Bank in a tender to sell the state shares in IPB, the first in a wave of bank privatisations being prepared by the Finance Ministry.
The deal should be completed by August 1, a government spokesman said on Thursday.

The state holds a 31.5 percent stake in IPB through the privatisation agency, the National Property Fund (NPF), and an additional 4.5 percent via the Czech Post Office. The Finance Minstry holds a further 0.3 percent.

Investors and international organisations have long been calling on the Czech government to push on with the privatisation of Czech banks which are generally perceived as lacking the competitive edge of foreign rivals.
Pilip told reporters that, if necessary for the stability of the bank, Nomura would be prepared to deposit up to 12 billion crowns in IPB.

On Tuesday, Pilip said he would submit proposals to the government for further state divestment in the other largest Czech banks -- Komercni Banka a.s., Ceska Sporitelna a.s. and Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka a.s.-- on August 20.
The IPB sale was delayed by a Finance Ministry investigation into the bank's investment subsidiary, Prvni Investicni a.s. (PIAS).
PIAS, the Czech Republic's largest fund manager, was earlier this month fined 10 million crowns, the maximum, for illegal financing operations and other violations.
The ministry also ordered changes in the management of PIAS and said it must cancel its contract making IPB its broker.

The privatisation process of IPB had already hit a snag when police arrested the bank's general director Jiri Tesar and his deputy for alleged fraud. The two have since been released from jail, but an investigation into the case continues. Tesar stepped down as director at IPB's annual general meeting.
IPB posted an 858 million crown net profit in 1996, according to Czech accounting standards, which it has said it expects to rise to 2.03 billion this year.
IPB shares gained seven crowns on the Prague Stock Exchange on Thursday after the news of the sell-off, to close at 243 crowns.
